title: Martin Zinkevich / Google, Rules of Machine Learning: Best Practices for ML Engineering
text:
## Core terminology
Google's Rules of ML fixes a shared vocabulary. An Instance is the thing you want to make a prediction about (for example a web page you want to classify). A Label is the answer to a prediction task, either the answer produced by an ML system or the true answer in training data. A Feature is a property of an instance used in prediction. A Feature Column is a set of related features (for example the set of all countries users could live in). An Example is an instance plus its features plus a label. A Model is a statistical representation of a prediction task, trained on examples then used to predict. A Metric is a number you care about. An Objective is a metric your algorithm is trying to optimize. A Pipeline is the infrastructure around an ML algorithm, including gathering data, putting data into training files, training models, and pushing them to production.

## Before machine learning
Rule #1: Don't be afraid to launch a product without machine learning. If ML is not strictly needed, do not use it until you have data. Rule #2: First, design and implement metrics. Instrument and track lots of things before formalizing what the ML system will do, because you will thank yourself later. Rule #3: Choose machine learning over a complex heuristic. A simple heuristic can get your product out the door, but a complex heuristic is unmaintainable, and once you have data and a basic idea, move to ML.

## Phase I: your first pipeline
Rule #4: Keep the first model simple and get the infrastructure right. The first model provides the biggest boost to your product, so it does not need to be fancy, but you will run into many more infrastructure issues than you expect. Rule #5: Test the infrastructure independently from the machine learning. Rule #6: Be careful about dropped data when copying pipelines. Rule #7: Turn heuristics into features, or handle them externally. Rule #8: Know the freshness requirements of your system. Rule #9: Detect problems before exporting models. Rule #10: Watch for silent failures. This is a problem more particular to ML systems than others: a table you were joining against stops being updated, or a feature quietly becomes stale, and the system slowly degrades while metrics look fine.

## Feature engineering and human analysis
Rule #16: Plan to launch and iterate. Do not expect the model you are working on now to be the last. Rule #17: Start with directly observed and reported features as opposed to learned features. Rule #20: Combine and modify existing features to create new features in human understandable ways. Rule #26: Look for patterns in the measured errors, and create new features. Rule #28: Be aware that identical short term behavior does not imply identical long term behavior.

## Training-serving skew
Rule #29: The best way to make sure that you train like you serve is to save the set of features used at serving time, and then pipe those features to a log to use them at training time. Rule #37: Measure Training and Serving Skew. Training-serving skew is a difference between performance during training and performance during serving, caused by a discrepancy between how you handle data in the training and serving pipelines, a change in the data between when you train and when you serve, or a feedback loop between your model and your algorithm.

## Slowed growth, optimization refinement, and complex models
Rule #38: Don't waste time on new features if unaligned objectives have become the issue. Rule #39: Launch decisions are a proxy for long term product goals. Rule #41: When performance plateaus, look for qualitatively new sources of information to add rather than refining existing signals. Rule #42: Don't expect diversity, personalization, or relevance to be as correlated with popularity as you think they are.

title: scikit-learn, Cross-validation: evaluating estimator performance
text:
## Why hold out a test set
Learning the parameters of a prediction function and testing it on the same data is a methodological mistake: a model that just repeats the labels of the samples it has seen would score perfectly but would fail to predict anything useful on yet unseen data. This situation is called overfitting. To avoid it, it is common practice to hold out part of the available data as a test set X_test, y_test. train_test_split is a convenience function for this.

## The leak from tuning on the test set
When evaluating different hyperparameters for estimators, such as the C setting for an SVM, there is still a risk of overfitting on the test set because the parameters can be tweaked until the estimator performs optimally. This way, knowledge about the test set can leak into the model and evaluation metrics no longer report on generalization performance. To solve this problem, yet another part of the dataset can be held out as a validation set: training proceeds on the training set, evaluation is done on the validation set, and when the experiment seems successful, final evaluation can be done on the test set. However, partitioning the available data into three sets drastically reduces the number of samples which can be used for learning the model.

## k-fold cross-validation
A solution is a procedure called cross-validation, or CV. A test set should still be held out for final evaluation, but the validation set is no longer needed when doing CV. In the basic approach, called k-fold CV, the training set is split into k smaller sets. For each of the k folds, a model is trained using k minus 1 of the folds as training data, and the resulting model is validated on the remaining part of the data. The performance measure reported by k-fold cross-validation is then the average of the values computed in the loop. This approach can be computationally expensive but does not waste too much data, which is a major advantage in problems such as inverse inference where the number of samples is very small. cross_val_score is the simplest way to use cross-validation. When the cv argument is an integer, cross_val_score uses the KFold or StratifiedKFold strategies by default, the latter being used if the estimator derives from ClassifierMixin.

## CV strategies
KFold divides all the samples into k groups of samples called folds of equal sizes. StratifiedKFold is a variation of k-fold which returns stratified folds, each containing approximately the same percentage of samples of each target class as the complete set, which matters for imbalanced classification. LeaveOneOut (LOO) leaves out one sample and trains on the rest, creating n different training sets for n samples. LOO does not waste much data but is computationally expensive and often results in high variance as an estimator for the test error; as a general rule, 5 or 10 fold cross validation should be preferred to LOO. GroupKFold ensures that the same group is not represented in both testing and training sets, which is essential when data is grouped (for example multiple samples from the same patient or subject). TimeSeriesSplit is a variation of k-fold for time dependent data: successive training sets are supersets of those that come before them, so the model is always tested on data that comes after the training window, respecting autocorrelation.

## Data leakage from preprocessing
Just as it is important to test a predictor on data held out from training, preprocessing such as standardization, feature selection, and similar transformations should be learnt from a training set and applied to held-out data for prediction. Fitting a scaler or feature selector on the whole dataset before cross-validation leaks information from the validation folds. To avoid this, a Pipeline makes it easier to compose estimators so that the preprocessing is learnt from the training folds only inside the cross-validation loop. permutation_test_score offers a way to check whether measured performance is real: it permutes the labels to generate a null distribution and reports a permutation based p-value; a low p-value means the dataset contains real dependency between features and labels.

title: scikit-learn, Metrics and scoring: quantifying the quality of predictions
text:
## Accuracy and why it misleads
accuracy_score computes the fraction of correct predictions over n_samples. Accuracy can be misleading on imbalanced datasets: if 99 percent of examples are negative, a model that always predicts negative scores 99 percent accuracy while catching zero positives. This is the accuracy paradox and is a reason to prefer precision, recall, balanced accuracy, or the Matthews correlation coefficient on skewed data.

## Confusion matrix
confusion_matrix returns a matrix where entry (i, j) is the number of observations actually in group i but predicted to be in group j. For the binary case the four cells are true negatives tn, false positives fp, false negatives fn, and true positives tp, retrievable via confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred).ravel().

## Precision, recall, and F measures
Precision is the ability of the classifier not to label as positive a sample that is negative, defined as tp divided by (tp plus fp). Recall, also called sensitivity, is the ability to find all the positive samples, defined as tp divided by (tp plus fn). The F-beta score is the weighted harmonic mean of precision and recall, F_beta equals (1 plus beta squared) times precision times recall divided by (beta squared times precision plus recall). The F1 score sets beta equal to 1, weighting precision and recall equally. beta less than 1 lends more weight to precision, beta greater than 1 favors recall. Functions include precision_score, recall_score, f1_score, fbeta_score, and precision_recall_fscore_support.

## Precision-recall curve and average precision
precision_recall_curve computes precision-recall pairs for different probability thresholds for binary classification. average_precision_score summarizes such a curve as the weighted mean of precisions achieved at each threshold, with the increase in recall from the previous threshold used as the weight: AP equals the sum over n of (R_n minus R_{n-1}) times P_n. With random predictions, AP is the fraction of positive samples.

## ROC and AUC
roc_curve plots the true positive rate (tp over (tp plus fn)) against the false positive rate (fp over (fp plus tn)) as the decision threshold varies. roc_auc_score computes the area under this curve. A key difference matters for imbalanced data: ROC AUC is invariant to class imbalance because both its axes are computed within the true positive and true negative groups, while precision-recall curves are more sensitive to imbalance and are recommended when the positive class is rare, because a large number of true negatives can make the ROC curve look optimistic.

## Averaging across classes
For multiclass and multilabel problems the average parameter controls aggregation. macro takes the unweighted mean of the per-class metric, giving equal weight to each class and so highlighting minority class performance. weighted averages per-class metrics weighted by the number of true instances of each class, accounting for imbalance. micro counts total true positives, false positives, and false negatives globally, so each sample-class pair contributes equally. Setting average to None returns the score per class.

## Probabilistic and agreement metrics
log_loss (cross-entropy loss) is the negative log-likelihood of the true labels given a probabilistic classifier's predictions and requires predict_proba output. brier_score_loss is the squared error between predicted probabilities and one-hot outcomes and is a strictly consistent scoring function, so truth telling is an optimal strategy in expectation. matthews_corrcoef (MCC) uses all four confusion matrix cells and returns a value in the range minus 1 to plus 1, where plus 1 is perfect prediction, 0 is random, and minus 1 is total disagreement; it is regarded as a balanced measure even when classes are of very different sizes. balanced_accuracy_score is the macro-average of recall obtained on each class and avoids inflated estimates on imbalanced data. cohen_kappa_score measures agreement between two annotators, where above 0.8 is generally considered good agreement and values at or below 0 mean no agreement beyond chance.

title: Wasserstein & Lazar, The ASA Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose (The American Statistician)
text:
## Informal definition
The American Statistical Association gives an informal definition of a p-value as the probability under a specified statistical model that a statistical summary of the data (for example, the sample mean difference between two compared groups) would be equal to or more extreme than its observed value. The statement was issued to improve the conduct and interpretation of quantitative science, in the context of concerns about reproducibility and the misuse of statistical significance.

## Principle 1: compatibility with a model
P-values can indicate how incompatible the data are with a specified statistical model. The smaller the p-value, the greater the statistical incompatibility of the data with the null hypothesis, if the underlying assumptions used to calculate the p-value hold. This incompatibility can be interpreted as casting doubt on or providing evidence against the null hypothesis or its assumptions.

## Principle 2: what a p-value is not
P-values do not measure the probability that the studied hypothesis is true, or the probability that the data were produced by random chance alone. A p-value is a statement about data in relation to a specified hypothetical explanation, and is not a statement about the explanation itself.

## Principle 3: do not decide on a threshold alone
Scientific conclusions and business or policy decisions should not be based only on whether a p-value passes a specific threshold. The widespread use of statistical significance, generally interpreted as p less than 0.05, as a license for making a claim of a scientific finding leads to considerable distortion of the scientific process. Decisions should consider context including the design of a study, the quality of the measurements, and the plausibility of the underlying mechanism.

## Principle 4: full reporting and transparency
Proper inference requires full reporting and transparency. P-values and related analyses should not be reported selectively. Conducting multiple analyses of the data and reporting only those with certain p-values, commonly known as p-hacking, data dredging, significance chasing, or cherry-picking, renders reported p-values essentially uninterpretable. Researchers should disclose the number of hypotheses explored, all data collection decisions, all statistical analyses conducted, and all p-values computed.

## Principle 5: significance is not effect size or importance
A p-value, or statistical significance, does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result. Smaller p-values do not necessarily imply the presence of larger or more important effects, and larger p-values do not imply a lack of importance or even lack of effect. Any effect, no matter how tiny, can produce a small p-value if the sample size or measurement precision is high enough.

## Principle 6: a p-value is limited evidence
By itself, a p-value does not provide a good measure of evidence regarding a model or hypothesis. A p-value near 0.05 taken by itself offers only weak evidence against the null hypothesis. Researchers should recognize that a p-value without context or other evidence provides limited information.

title: scikit-learn, Underfitting vs. Overfitting (bias-variance tradeoff example)
text:
## Underfitting and high bias
Underfitting happens when a model is too simple to capture the underlying structure of the data. In the scikit-learn example that fits polynomial features of increasing degree to a cosine function, a linear function of polynomial degree 1 is not sufficient to fit the training samples, producing a high mean squared error of about 4.08e-01. An underfit model has high bias: it makes strong assumptions and cannot approximate the true function, so it performs poorly on both training and validation data.

## Overfitting and high variance
Overfitting happens when a model is so flexible that it learns the noise in the training data instead of the underlying pattern. In the same example a polynomial of degree 15 learns the noise of the training data, so it fits the sampled points closely but generalizes poorly to unseen data. An overfit model has high variance: small changes in the training set produce large changes in the fitted function.

## The bias-variance tradeoff and the sweet spot
Between these extremes there is a model of the right complexity. A polynomial of degree 4 approximates the true function almost perfectly, with the lowest validation error of about 4.32e-02. The key evaluation method is cross-validation: the example uses cross_val_score with scoring set to negative mean squared error and cv equal to 10 to quantify how well each candidate generalizes, choosing complexity by minimizing validation error rather than training error. This is the practical form of the bias-variance tradeoff: too little complexity means high bias and underfitting, too much means high variance and overfitting, and the goal is the complexity that minimizes total error on held-out data.

title: Kohavi, Deng, Frasca, Longbotham, Walker, Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: Five Puzzling Outcomes Explained (KDD 2012)
text:
## What an online controlled experiment is
An online controlled experiment, commonly called an A/B test, is a randomized trial in which users are randomly split into a control group that sees the current experience and one or more treatment groups that see a variant. Because assignment is random, differences in the metrics between the groups can be attributed causally to the change being tested rather than to confounding factors. These experiments are the primary way large online companies make data driven product decisions.

## Overall Evaluation Criterion (OEC)
The OEC is the single quantitative metric, or small set of metrics, agreed upon in advance to evaluate whether a treatment is better than control. A good OEC captures long term value to the business rather than a short term proxy that can be gamed. The paper stresses choosing the OEC carefully because teams optimize whatever the OEC rewards.

## Small effects matter at scale
At the scale of large online services, even very small relative improvements in a key metric translate into large absolute value, so experiments are designed with enough statistical power to reliably detect small changes. This is why sample sizes are large and why properly powered tests, run long enough, are essential.

## Primacy and novelty effects
When a change is introduced, existing users may react to the change itself rather than to its lasting value. A novelty effect is a temporary boost because a new feature attracts attention that fades over time. A primacy effect is the opposite: experienced users are initially slowed or resistant because they are used to the old way, and the treatment looks worse at first before improving. Both mean the treatment effect can change over time, so an experiment should run long enough for behavior to stabilize before a decision is made.

## Twyman's law and skepticism
The paper invokes Twyman's law: any figure that looks interesting or different is usually wrong. Surprising or extreme experimental results should trigger investigation for instrumentation bugs, tracking loss, or data problems before they are believed. Trust in an experimentation system depends on catching these before acting.

## Carryover effects and reusing populations
Carryover effects occur when a previous experiment leaves a lasting impact on users that contaminates a later experiment run on the same population. Re-randomizing users and being aware of carryover is important so that residual effects from a prior treatment are not mistaken for the effect of the current one.

title: Kaufman, Rosset, Perlich, Leakage in Data Mining: Formulation, Detection, and Avoidance (KDD 2011)
text:
## Definition of leakage
Leakage is defined as the introduction of information about the data mining target that should not be legitimately available to mine from. It is considered one of the top data mining mistakes. A model built on leaked information appears to perform excellently during evaluation because it has effectively seen the answer, but it fails when deployed, because that information is not actually available at prediction time.

## Two forms of leakage
The paper distinguishes leakage in features, where the feature set contains direct or derivative information about the target that would not exist in a real prediction scenario, from leakage in training examples, where information from the evaluation or future period leaks into the training data and violates temporal boundaries. The unifying rule is a no-time-machine requirement: a legitimate model may only use information available at the moment the prediction has to be made, and cannot use information from the future to predict the present.

## Concrete examples
A classic case is the KDD Cup 2008 breast cancer detection task, where a patient identifier carried information about the source institution and therefore about whether patients were likely to have cancer, letting models exploit the ID rather than the medical imaging features. Another example is an account number or record identifier whose numbering encodes historical outcome information, creating a phantom predictive signal that vanishes on genuinely new records. In these cases the leaking feature is highly predictive in backtesting but useless or misleading in production.

## Detection and avoidance
Avoiding leakage requires assessing the legitimacy of every feature: would this information realistically exist, with these values, at the time the prediction must be made. The authors recommend a strict learn-predict separation in time so that training data precedes the prediction decision point, and they distinguish internal leakage introduced during feature engineering from external contamination in the data sources. Suspiciously high cross-validation performance, or a single feature that dominates the model, are practical warning signs to investigate for leakage before trusting a result.

title: Evan Miller, How Not To Run An A/B Test (the peeking problem)
text:
## The peeking problem
Most A/B testing software reports a significance level, but that calculation assumes the sample size was fixed in advance. If instead you run a test and stop it as soon as it reaches significance, watching the results continuously and calling the winner early, the reported significance levels are meaningless. Repeatedly testing for significance and stopping at the first significant result is a form of multiple comparisons that inflates the false positive rate far above the nominal level.

## The inflated error rates
Evan Miller gives concrete numbers. In the worst case, testing after every single observation with a 5 percent target significance level produces an actual false positive rate of about 26.1 percent, more than five times what the experimenter thinks they are getting. He also tabulates how much stricter the reported threshold must be to keep the true error at 5 percent when peeking: roughly 2.9 percent reported significance if you peek once, and about 1.0 percent if you peek ten times. The more you peek, the more your significance levels will be off.

## The fix
The primary fix is to decide the sample size in advance and stick to that sample size with near religious discipline, not stopping early just because the result looks significant. A rule of thumb for the required sample size per variation is n equals 16 times sigma squared divided by delta squared, where delta is the minimum effect you want to detect and sigma squared is the sample variance. Alternatives that do allow continuous monitoring are proper sequential experiment designs with predetermined checkpoints and corrected thresholds, or Bayesian methods designed to permit optional stopping. The key discipline is that you may not simply stop an ordinary fixed-horizon test the moment it crosses p less than 0.05.

title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Simpson's Paradox
text:
## Definition
Simpson's paradox occurs when an association between two variables in a population emerges, disappears, or reverses when the population is divided into subpopulations. A relationship visible in the aggregate data can completely reverse when you examine the subgroups separately, or two variables that look positively associated overall can be independent or negatively associated within every subgroup.

## A medical example
A foundational case involves treatment that appears equally effective in aggregate, 20 of 40 successes in each group for a 50 percent rate, yet shows a higher success rate for treatment within each gender stratum: about 61 percent for treated men versus 57 percent for control men, and 44 percent for treated women versus 40 percent for control women. Treatment looks better in both subgroups yet no better in the pooled data, because gender is correlated with treatment assignment in the sample.

## The confounding variable
The reversal arises from correlations between the treatment variable and the partitioning variable. Gender acts as a confounding factor: it independently influences both who received treatment and who recovered. Because subgroup sizes differ systematically by treatment, the weighted averages that make up the aggregate statistics can reverse the apparent relationship. This is why the probabilistic relationship in pooled data may be evidential rather than causal.

## The Berkeley admissions case
The most famous instance is the UC Berkeley graduate admissions data, where men were admitted at a higher overall rate, yet the original authors could not detect a bias toward men in any individual department. Women had applied disproportionately to more competitive departments with lower acceptance rates for all applicants, so the aggregate gap was driven by which departments each group applied to, not by discrimination within departments.

## Practical lesson
The lesson for a data scientist is that you cannot trust a pooled association without asking whether a lurking third variable differs across the groups being compared. Deciding whether to analyze aggregated or disaggregated data is a causal question, not a purely statistical one: you should condition on genuine confounders and avoid conditioning on variables that lie on the causal path. Randomized assignment, or a design with equal treatment-to-control ratios within every subgroup, removes the correlation between treatment and the confounder and prevents the paradox.

title: Nick Huntington-Klein, The Effect: Causal Diagrams
text:
## What a causal diagram is
A causal diagram, or directed acyclic graph, is a visual model of the data generating process. It contains the variables in the process and the causal relationships between them. Each variable is a single node, drawn as a circle regardless of how many values it takes, and arrows point from causes to effects. An arrow only tells us that one variable causes another; it says nothing about whether that effect is positive or negative. Every variable and arrow that is not on the diagram is an assumption you are making, which forces you to state your assumptions and makes them open to scrutiny.

## Definition of causality
The working definition is that X causes Y if, by intervening to change X, the distribution of Y changes as a result. This distinguishes causation from correlation. A standard example is that wearing shorts does not cause you to eat ice cream and ice cream does not cause you to wear shorts, yet the two are correlated because temperature is a common cause of both.

## Confounders and back-door paths
A confounder is a variable that causes both the treatment and the outcome. It opens a back-door path, a non-causal route connecting treatment and outcome that generates a spurious association. In a policing example, past crime causes both current police presence and current crime, confounding the relationship between police and crime. To recover the true effect you must block these back-door paths, usually by controlling for the confounder.

## Colliders
A collider is a variable that is caused by two others, drawn as two arrows pointing into the same node. A collider naturally blocks the path that runs through it, so you should leave it alone. Controlling for or conditioning on a collider does the opposite of controlling for a confounder: it opens the path and can create a spurious association between the collider's two causes even when they are otherwise unrelated. This is why controlling for more variables is not always better.

## Identification
Identification means isolating just the variation you need to answer the causal question of interest. You keep the causal paths from treatment to outcome open while closing every non-causal path, in particular the back-door paths through confounders, and you avoid opening paths by conditioning on colliders. When all non-causal paths are closed and the causal path remains open, the remaining association identifies the causal effect.

title: Alex Reinhart, Statistics Done Wrong: Statistical power and underpowered statistics
text:
## What statistical power is
Statistical power is the probability that a study will detect an effect of a certain size, distinguishing it from pure luck, when that effect really exists. Equivalently it is the probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis when the alternative is true, so it is one minus the Type II (false negative) error rate. A study with low power will frequently fail to find real effects.

## What power depends on
Power depends on three things: the size of the effect you are trying to detect, the sample size, and the significance threshold. Larger effects are easier to detect than subtle ones, and larger samples give more power. A coin-flip example shows the point: with only 10 flips, detecting a coin biased to 60 percent heads has just about 20 percent power, while with 100 or 1,000 flips detecting the same bias becomes nearly certain. Researchers typically aim for power of 0.8 or higher, an 80 percent chance of detecting a real effect.

## The consequences of underpowered studies
Underpowered studies routinely miss real effects. In a sample of medical trials, 27 percent of randomized controlled trials reported negative results, but 64 percent of those did not collect enough data to detect even a 50 percent difference in the primary outcome, and 84 percent could not detect a 25 percent difference. In neuroscience the median study has been estimated to have only about a 20 percent chance of detecting the effect it is looking for. A key insight is that concluding no statistically significant difference does not mean no real difference exists; the study may simply be too small to detect it.

## Truth inflation and the winner's curse
Underpowered studies also distort the effects they do find. When power is low, only unusually large sample estimates cross the significance threshold, so the statistically significant results that get published systematically overstate the true effect size. This truth inflation, or winner's curse, means an effect that barely reaches significance in a small study is likely exaggerated. The remedy is to run a power and sample-size calculation before collecting data, choosing a sample large enough to detect the smallest effect that would matter.

title: Head, Holman, Lanfear, Kahn, Jennions, The Extent and Consequences of P-Hacking in Science (PLOS Biology)
text:
## Definition of p-hacking
P-hacking, also called selective reporting or inflation bias, occurs when researchers collect or select data or statistical analyses until nonsignificant results become significant. It exploits the flexibility in how data are gathered and analyzed, the so-called researcher degrees of freedom, to push a p-value below the 0.05 threshold rather than to test a pre-specified hypothesis honestly.

## Common p-hacking behaviors
The paper lists concrete practices that constitute p-hacking: conducting analyses midway through data collection to decide whether to continue; recording many response variables and deciding which to report only after seeing which are significant; deciding post hoc whether to include or exclude observations or outliers; excluding, combining, or splitting treatment groups after looking at the results; selectively including or dropping covariates; and stopping data collection once a significant result is reached. Each of these lets a researcher search across many possible analyses and report only the ones that worked.

## Method: the p-curve
The authors detected p-hacking at scale using the distribution of reported p-values, called the p-curve. They text-mined p-values from a very large set of open access papers across scientific disciplines, and separately analyzed p-values drawn from published meta-analyses. A genuine population of true effects produces a right-skewed p-curve with many very small p-values, whereas widespread p-hacking leaves a telltale bump of p-values just under 0.05.

## Findings
They found evidence of p-hacking across the scientific literature, with a detectable excess of p-values just below 0.05 in multiple fields. However, they concluded that although p-hacking appears widespread, it probably does not drastically alter the broad conclusions drawn from meta-analyses, in part because the smaller studies most prone to p-hacking receive less weight in meta-analytic estimates. The practical lesson is that a single significant result, especially one that barely clears 0.05, is weak evidence, and that pre-registration and full disclosure of analyses are the defenses against this failure mode.

title: Data Science Process Alliance, What is CRISP-DM (the six phases)
text:
## What CRISP-DM is
CRISP-DM, the Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining, is the most widely used framework for organizing a data science or data mining project. It breaks the work into six phases. The sequence of the phases is not rigid: moving back and forth between different phases is always required, so the process is iterative and cyclical rather than a one-way waterfall.

## Business Understanding
The project starts by understanding the business. This phase determines the business objectives and success criteria, assesses the situation including resources, requirements, risks, and a cost-benefit analysis, translates the business goal into a data mining goal, and produces a project plan. Getting this phase right prevents solving the wrong problem well.

## Data Understanding
This phase collects the initial data, describes its properties such as format, record count, and field identities, explores the data through queries and visualization to find relationships, and verifies data quality, documenting any issues found.

## Data Preparation
Data Preparation selects which data to use with documented justification, cleans the data by correcting, imputing, or removing erroneous values, constructs new attributes, integrates data from multiple sources, and formats it for the modeling tools. A common rule of thumb is that 80 percent of the project is data preparation, making this the most time-consuming phase.

## Modeling
Modeling selects modeling techniques such as regression or neural networks, generates a test design by splitting data into training, test, and validation sets, builds the model, and assesses model performance against the success criteria. Different techniques may impose different data requirements, so this phase can loop back to Data Preparation.

## Evaluation and Deployment
Evaluation assesses the results against the business success criteria, not just the statistical metrics, reviews the process for oversights, and decides whether to deploy, iterate, or start a new project. Deployment plans the rollout, plans monitoring and maintenance for the operational phase, produces the final report, and conducts a retrospective. The step that turns a model into value is deployment plus ongoing monitoring, which is why it is a named phase and not an afterthought.

title: Google Machine Learning Crash Course, Regularization
text:
## What regularization does
Regularization is a mechanism that penalizes model complexity in order to reduce overfitting. Instead of training a model to minimize loss alone, which tends to memorize the training data, regularization follows the principle of structural risk minimization: minimize loss plus complexity. A scalar called the regularization rate, written lambda, multiplies the complexity term, so the objective becomes minimize loss plus lambda times complexity.

## L2 regularization
L2 regularization, also called ridge, defines complexity as the sum of the squared weights, w1 squared plus w2 squared and so on. L2 encourages weights toward 0 but never pushes weights all the way to zero, so every feature keeps some contribution. A high regularization rate tends to produce a histogram of model weights that is roughly a normal distribution with a mean weight of 0. L1 regularization, by contrast, penalizes the absolute value of the weights and can drive weights to exactly zero, producing sparsity and acting as a form of feature selection.

## Choosing lambda
The regularization rate controls a tradeoff. A high lambda strengthens regularization and reduces overfitting risk, but if it is too high the model underfits and cannot learn the signal. A low lambda lowers the influence of regularization and increases the chance of overfitting, and setting lambda to zero removes regularization entirely, maximizing overfitting risk. There is also an equilibrium with the learning rate: a high learning rate pulls weights away from zero while a high regularization rate pushes them toward zero, so the two must be balanced. You tune lambda on a validation set.

## Early stopping
Early stopping is an alternative to an explicit penalty term. It means ending training before the model fully converges, typically when validation loss stops improving and begins to increase. Early stopping usually raises training loss but can lower test loss, because it prevents the model from continuing to fit noise in the training data.

title: Max Kuhn & Kjell Johnson, Feature Engineering and Selection: A Practical Approach for Predictive Models
text:
## What feature engineering is
Feature engineering is the process of adjusting and creating representations of the predictors so that a model can better uncover the relationship between the predictors and the response. Often the relevant predictors are collected but are represented in a way that makes it hard for a model to achieve good performance. How predictors are encoded can be as influential as, or more influential than, the choice of modeling algorithm itself.

## Types of encodings
Useful relationships can involve transformations of individual predictors, interactions between two or more predictors such as products or ratios, functional relationships among predictors, and alternative representations of an existing predictor. Common examples include breaking a date into components like day of week and month, converting counts into rates, log-transforming skewed variables, and encoding categorical variables. The goal is to expose the underlying signal in a form the model can use.

## It is model dependent and part art
The optimal representation depends on the specific model being used, so what helps a linear model may be unnecessary for a tree-based model that can split on raw values. Although it is called engineering, the authors describe it as more of an art that requires the right tools and experience, since practitioners typically must search many alternative predictor representations to improve performance.

## Avoid leakage: engineer inside resampling
A critical discipline is to perform feature engineering inside the resampling loop rather than once on the full dataset. Estimating transformations, imputations, or encodings using the entire dataset, including the held-out folds, leaks information and produces optimistic performance estimates. By re-deriving every learned preprocessing step from the training portion of each resample, the estimated performance honestly reflects how the pipeline will behave on new data.

title: Greenland, Senn, Rothman, Carlin, Poole, Goodman, Altman, Statistical tests, P values, confidence intervals, and power: a guide to misinterpretations
text:
## The correct definition of a p-value
Greenland and colleagues define a p-value as the probability that the chosen test statistic would have been at least as large as its observed value if every model assumption, including the test hypothesis, were correct. It measures the compatibility between the observed data and what we would expect to see if the entire statistical model were correct. Crucially, the p-value assumes the test hypothesis is true; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.

## P value is not the probability the null is true
Misinterpretation: the p-value is the probability that the test hypothesis is true, so that P equals 0.01 means the null hypothesis has only a 1 percent chance of being true. This is false. The p-value assumes the test hypothesis is true and is not a hypothesis probability; it may be far from any reasonable probability for the test hypothesis.

## Nonsignificant does not prove the null
Misinterpretation: a nonsignificant result, P greater than 0.05, means that the test hypothesis is true or should be accepted. This is false. A large p-value only indicates that the data are not unusual if all the assumptions used to compute it, including the test hypothesis, were correct. Related misinterpretation: a null p-value greater than 0.05 means that no effect was observed or that absence of an effect was demonstrated. This is also false, because observing P greater than 0.05 for the null only means the null is one among many hypotheses with P greater than 0.05.

## Significant does not mean important
Misinterpretation: statistical significance indicates that a scientifically or substantively important relation has been detected. This is false, because very minor effects or small assumption violations can lead to statistically significant tests when the sample is large. Judging importance requires looking at the effect size and its confidence interval, not the p-value.

## What a confidence interval really means
Misinterpretation: the specific 95 percent confidence interval presented by a study has a 95 percent chance of containing the true effect size. This is false. The 95 percent refers only to how often 95 percent confidence intervals computed from very many studies would contain the true value if all the assumptions used to compute the intervals were correct. Any single computed interval either contains the true value or it does not; the confidence level is a property of the procedure over repeated sampling, not of the one interval in hand.

title: Summary of Benjamini & Hochberg (1995), Controlling the False Discovery Rate
text:
## The multiple testing problem
When you test many hypotheses at once, the chance of at least one false positive grows quickly. If you run 20 independent tests each at the 0.05 level and everything is truly null, you expect about one significant result by chance alone. Some correction is needed when reporting the results of many comparisons, otherwise significant findings are largely noise.

## Family-wise error rate and Bonferroni
The family-wise error rate (FWER) is the probability of making at least one false discovery across all the tests. The Bonferroni correction controls FWER by testing each of m hypotheses at level alpha divided by m. This guarantees strong control of the FWER but is overly stringent: as the number of tests grows, the per-test threshold becomes tiny, so power to detect real effects collapses and many true signals are missed.

## The false discovery rate
Benjamini and Hochberg proposed a different, less conservative criterion: the false discovery rate (FDR), the expected proportion of false discoveries among all discoveries, written as the expectation of V over R, where V is the number of true null hypotheses rejected and R is the total number rejected. Controlling FDR at a level q means you accept that, on average, at most a fraction q of your declared discoveries are false, which is often the right tradeoff when you are screening many candidates and can tolerate a controlled share of false leads.

## The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure
The BH step-up procedure works as follows: order the p-values from smallest to largest as p(1) up to p(m); find the largest index k such that p(k) is less than or equal to (k divided by m) times q; then reject all hypotheses with p-values up to and including p(k). This detects more true positives than Bonferroni while still controlling the error at the chosen FDR level q, which is why FDR control became standard in large-scale testing such as genomics and in A/B testing programs that run many metrics at once.

title: imbalanced-learn, Introduction (resampling for imbalanced classification)
text:
## What class imbalance is and why it hurts
Class imbalance is when a dataset contains very unequal numbers of samples across classes, for example fraud or disease detection where the positive class is rare. When a classifier is trained on imbalanced data it develops a systematic bias toward the majority class: as imbalance increases, a logistic regression decision function tends to favour the class with the larger number of samples. This is why plain accuracy is unreliable on imbalanced data, since a model can score high accuracy while almost never predicting the minority class, and metrics like recall, precision, balanced accuracy, F1, and the area under the precision-recall curve are preferred.

## Over-sampling
Over-sampling methods add minority-class examples so the classes are more balanced. RandomOverSampler duplicates existing minority samples at random. SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique) creates new synthetic minority samples by interpolating between a minority point and its nearest neighbours. ADASYN is a related method that generates more synthetic samples in the harder-to-learn regions near the decision boundary.

## Under-sampling
Under-sampling methods remove majority-class examples. RandomUnderSampler drops majority samples at random. Tomek links removes borderline majority samples that are nearest neighbours of a minority sample of the opposite class. NearMiss selects majority samples based on their distance to minority samples, and Edited Nearest Neighbours removes majority samples whose class disagrees with their neighbours.

## Combination and ensemble methods
Combination methods apply over and under-sampling in sequence, such as SMOTEENN and SMOTETomek, to both grow the minority class and clean noisy borderline points. Ensemble approaches build balanced subsets across multiple learners, including BalancedRandomForestClassifier and EasyEnsemble.

## The leakage warning
A critical implementation rule is that resampling must be applied only to the training data, inside a pipeline, and never to the validation or test data. Resampling before splitting, or resampling the whole dataset, leaks information and artificially inflates the performance you measure. The imbalanced-learn Pipeline is designed so that samplers run only on the training fold during cross-validation.

title: Convert, Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) Guide
text:
## What a sample ratio mismatch is
Sample Ratio Mismatch, or SRM, occurs when the actual distribution of users across test variants diverges significantly from the expected allocation. For example, a test configured for a 50/50 split might instead observe about 60 percent of users in one variant and 40 percent in the other. That deviation is a symptom that something is wrong with the experiment machinery, not a result you should interpret.

## Why SRM invalidates a test
Random assignment is the backbone of A/B testing: it is what lets you attribute observed differences between groups to your change rather than to some confounder. SRM breaks that link. When the randomization or logging that produces the split is broken, the two groups are no longer comparable, so the treatment effect estimate is untrustworthy regardless of how sophisticated the statistics are. An experiment with a real SRM should be diagnosed and fixed, not shipped.

## How to detect it
The standard detection tool is a chi-squared goodness-of-fit test comparing the observed sample sizes in each variant against the expected sizes from the configured split. If the p-value is below 0.01, there is strong statistical evidence that the mismatch did not happen by chance. Because a mature program runs many experiments, this SRM check is used as a guardrail applied to every experiment before the results are read, with a strict threshold (commonly 0.01 or 0.001) to keep false alarms low.

## Common root causes
Root causes fall into a few families: assignment issues such as faulty randomization logic, user ID collisions, or non-deterministic bucketing; execution problems such as missing test scripts, incorrect targeting rules, or one variant launching before the other; logging failures such as bot traffic, user-agent mismatches, or incomplete data collection; analysis errors such as broken exposure or trigger tracking; and interference such as paused variations, concurrent overlapping experiments, or mid-test site changes. Because an SRM is a symptom of many possible bugs, detecting it is easy but finding and fixing the true cause is often the hard part.

title: Wikipedia, HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known)
text:
## Definition
HARKing stands for Hypothesizing After the Results are Known. The term was coined by social psychologist Norbert Kerr in a 1998 article, and refers to presenting a post hoc hypothesis in the introduction of a research report as if it were an a priori hypothesis. In other words, the researcher runs the analysis, sees which comparison came out significant, then writes up a hypothesis that predicts exactly that result, hiding the fact that the hypothesis was chosen after seeing the data.

## Why it is a problem
HARKing is a questionable research practice because post hoc hypothesizing is falsely portrayed as a priori hypothesizing, which distorts the fundamental distinction between exploratory and confirmatory research. Researchers who HARK may suppress the hypotheses they started with that gave nonsignificant results, and retrofit an explanation to whatever unexpected finding appeared. This capitalizes on chance and inflates false positive findings, because a result that only turned up because many possibilities were explored is presented as a confirmed prediction. It is a close cousin of p-hacking: p-hacking searches over analyses to get a small p-value, while HARKing rewrites the hypothesis to fit the result already found.

## The remedy
The main proposed defense is pre-registration of the research hypotheses and analysis plan before data collection, which pins down in advance what was predicted and how it would be tested. For a data scientist this maps directly onto separating exploratory analysis, where generating hypotheses from the data is legitimate, from confirmatory analysis, where a pre-specified hypothesis is tested on fresh data. Findings discovered while exploring should be validated on a new sample or a holdout before they are reported as confirmed.

title: scikit-learn, Regression metrics (Metrics and scoring)
text:
## The regression metric catalog
scikit-learn exposes a family of regression metrics, each with a scoring string and a function: r2_score for the coefficient of determination, mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, root_mean_squared_error, mean_squared_log_error, median_absolute_error, mean_absolute_percentage_error, explained_variance_score, max_error, and deviance measures like mean_poisson_deviance and mean_gamma_deviance. The scoring strings used with cross-validation are negated for the error metrics, for example neg_mean_absolute_error and neg_root_mean_squared_error, so that higher is always better for a scorer.

## R squared
r2_score computes the coefficient of determination, R squared, which represents the proportion of variance in the target explained by the model. A model that always predicts the mean of the target achieves an R squared of 0, a perfect model achieves 1, and an arbitrarily bad model can be negative. Because it is scale-free it is convenient for comparing across problems, but it can be misleading on non-linear relationships or when the test distribution differs from training.

## Absolute versus squared error
mean_absolute_error (MAE) is the average of the absolute differences between predictions and targets. Because it does not square the errors, it is more robust to outliers and reports error in the same units as the target. mean_squared_error (MSE) averages the squared errors, so it penalizes large errors much more heavily than small ones, and root_mean_squared_error (RMSE) is its square root, back on the original scale. Choosing between MAE and RMSE encodes how much you care about occasional large misses.

## Consistency and other metrics
The docs note strictly consistent scoring functions: the mean is elicited by squared error, the median by absolute error, and a quantile by pinball loss, meaning that predicting that summary is the optimal strategy in expectation under that loss. mean_absolute_percentage_error (MAPE) expresses error as a fraction of the true value and is sensitive to targets near zero. median_absolute_error is highly robust to outliers because it takes the median rather than the mean of the absolute errors. mean_squared_log_error penalizes underestimates and relative errors and suits targets that span several orders of magnitude.

title: Nick Huntington-Klein, The Effect: Difference-in-Differences
text:
## The setup
Difference-in-Differences (DiD) is a quasi-experimental method for estimating a causal effect when you cannot randomize. It compares a treated group that receives an intervention against a control or untreated group that does not, observed in a pre-period before treatment and a post-period after treatment. You compute four averages: treated before, treated after, control before, and control after.

## The core logic
The estimator is the difference of two differences: (treated group after minus treated group before) minus (untreated group after minus untreated group before). The control group's before-to-after change stands in for what would have happened to the treated group anyway, absent the intervention, because of general time trends. Subtracting it leaves only the change attributable to the treatment. Equivalently, the first difference removes fixed differences between the groups, and the second difference removes the common time trend.

## The parallel trends assumption
The key identifying assumption is parallel trends: had no treatment occurred, the gap between the treated and untreated groups would have remained constant over time, so the two groups would have moved in parallel. This assumption is unobservable, since you never see the treated group's untreated post-period, which is why practitioners examine pre-treatment trends and event-study plots as supporting evidence. If the groups were already diverging before treatment, DiD is biased.

## Regression form and time-invariant confounders
The 2 by 2 DiD can be written as a regression with an interaction term: Y equals beta0 plus beta1 times TreatedGroup plus beta2 times AfterTreatment plus beta3 times (TreatedGroup times AfterTreatment), where beta3 is the DiD effect. Group fixed effects absorb every confounder that is constant within a group over time, whether measured or not, which is the method's main strength: it controls for stable unobserved differences between the groups. It does not, however, control for confounders that change differently across the groups over time, which is exactly what the parallel trends assumption rules out.

title: scikit-learn, Ensemble methods (bagging, random forests, boosting)
text:
## Two families of ensembles
Ensemble methods combine the predictions of several base estimators to improve generalization and robustness over a single estimator. There are two fundamental families. Averaging or bagging methods build several estimators independently and then average their predictions; because the combined estimator has lower variance than any single member, bagging mainly reduces overfitting. Boosting methods build base estimators sequentially, each one trying to reduce the bias of the combined estimator, so a strong model is assembled from many weak learners.

## Bagging and random forests
The BaggingClassifier trains each estimator on a bootstrap sample, a random draw of the training rows with replacement, and averages them; the leftover rows give an out-of-bag score via oob_score that estimates generalization without a separate validation set. RandomForestClassifier extends bagging of decision trees by also choosing a random subset of features at each split (for classification, commonly the square root of the number of features), which decorrelates the trees so their averaged prediction has even lower variance. ExtraTrees (extremely randomized trees) go further and pick split thresholds at random. Random forests expose feature_importances_, though impurity-based importance is biased toward high-cardinality features and permutation_importance is a more reliable alternative.

## Boosting and gradient boosting
AdaBoost reweights misclassified samples so that later estimators focus on the hard cases. GradientBoosting fits each new tree to the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions, which for squared error is just the residual errors, and adds it with a shrinkage factor called the learning_rate; smaller learning rates need more trees but generalize better. Stochastic gradient boosting adds row and feature subsampling for regularization. HistGradientBoostingClassifier is a histogram-based variant that bins features and can be orders of magnitude faster than GradientBoostingClassifier when the number of samples is larger than tens of thousands, with native support for missing values and categorical features. Gradient-boosted trees are among the strongest models for tabular data.

## Combining models
StackingClassifier trains several diverse base estimators and then trains a final estimator on their cross-validated predictions, learning how best to combine them. VotingClassifier combines conceptually different fitted models by majority vote (hard voting) or by averaging predicted probabilities (soft voting), optionally with weights.

title: Scott Cunningham, Causal Inference: The Mixtape, Potential Outcomes Model
text:
## Potential outcomes notation
The potential outcomes framework, also called the Rubin causal model, assigns each unit two potential outcomes: Y to the power 1, the outcome if the unit is treated, and Y to the power 0, the outcome if it is not treated. These are two separate states of the world for the exact same person at the exact same moment in time, so at most one of them can ever be realized.

## Individual treatment effect and the fundamental problem
The unit-level causal effect is delta_i equals Y_i to the power 1 minus Y_i to the power 0, the difference between that unit's treated and untreated potential outcomes. The fundamental problem of causal inference is that we only ever observe one of the two potential outcomes for each unit, never both, so the individual treatment effect is unobservable. What we observe is governed by the switching equation Y_i equals D_i times Y_i to the power 1 plus (1 minus D_i) times Y_i to the power 0, where D_i is 1 if treated and 0 if not: when D_i equals 1 we see Y to the power 1 and the untreated outcome is missing, and vice versa. Certainty about causal effects would require data that is and always will be missing.

## Average effects and selection bias
Because individual effects are hidden, causal inference targets averages. The average treatment effect ATE is E of Y to the power 1 minus E of Y to the power 0. The average treatment effect on the treated ATT is E of (Y to the power 1 minus Y to the power 0 given D equals 1). A naive comparison of observed treated and untreated means does not recover the ATE: the simple difference in means decomposes into the ATE plus selection bias plus a heterogeneous treatment effect bias term. Selection bias is the difference in the untreated potential outcome between the groups, that is, how different the treated and control units already were before any treatment.

## SUTVA
The potential outcomes framework relies on the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA): each unit's potential outcome depends only on its own treatment, not on the treatment of other units (no interference or spillovers), and there is only one version of the treatment (a stable, homogeneous dose). SUTVA can be violated by network effects, marketplace or general equilibrium effects, and inconsistent treatment delivery, all of which a data scientist running experiments must watch for.
